**Evaluate whether the agent achieved the task, not whether its final message sounds convincing.** An agent can claim “I updated the spreadsheet” without changing any cells, or complete the task while producing an awkward summary. Evaluation therefore needs the initial state, allowed actions, and verifiable final-state conditions.

**Use a miniature task.** Suppose the agent must find an overdue invoice and create a draft reminder without sending it. Success requires selecting the correct invoice and recipient, creating a correct draft, and leaving the send state unchanged. Checking only whether the final text mentions the invoice would miss both a wrong-recipient draft and an unauthorized send.

**Make replay possible.** Snapshot the starting environment, version the tools and model, and save tool calls plus results. Reset between runs so one attempt does not alter the next. Use controlled external responses where live systems would make evaluation nondeterministic. [5](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents)

Some outcomes can be checked programmatically; others need a human or calibrated model judge. Judges can disagree or be fooled, so validate them on examples with known outcomes and inspect failures. Separate task success, cost, latency, policy violations, and recovery ability rather than hiding everything in one score.

**Test imperfect conditions.** Include timeouts, missing fields, ambiguous instructions, and failed tool calls. A useful agent should recover safely or state what prevented completion. Repeating a single easy benchmark until it scores highly can overfit the evaluator rather than improve real reliability.

**Technical details and references.**

A test case should define an initial environment snapshot, user objective, allowed tools, expected final-state properties, and a budget. Version the prompt, model, tools, evaluator, and dataset together. Run each candidate in an isolated resettable environment; save tool calls, observations, timings, costs, and final state so a failure is reproducible.

Use deterministic graders for facts that code can verify: a record was updated correctly, a file exists, a prohibited write never happened, or a budget was respected. Use a calibrated LLM judge for genuinely subjective quality, with a rubric, evidence, and blinded/randomized candidate order. Judge output is another measurement with error, not ground truth. Audit disagreement against human labels and prevent trajectories from instructing the grader.

Repeat stochastic tasks to estimate reliability and report confidence intervals, not only a single pass rate. Track success under budget, policy violations, unnecessary actions, and recovery after injected tool failures. Partition by task family and risk; keep a frozen regression set plus a changing production-derived set. Gate rollout on critical regressions, and retain historical trajectories to distinguish model changes from evaluator drift.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** Define success as verifiable final-state properties and report success rate with uncertainty across independent tasks/seeds. Also record cost, invalid tool calls, recovery, and unintended state changes. A judge score is a measurement instrument requiring calibration against human or executable checks; optimizing only that score can reward evaluator loopholes rather than successful work.
